questions.question: What is the main purpose of exploring data before applying a machine-learning method?
choices: To understand its patterns and problems before choosing an approach
To guarantee that the chosen model will be accurate
To remove all unusual observations automatically
To replace the need for testing the model
questions.explanation: The lecture frames exploration as making sense of data first. It informs later choices but does not guarantee accuracy.

questions.question: A feature has a much larger numerical spread than other features and dominates a distance-based clustering result. What should you have checked before clustering?
choices: Whether the chart has a title
questions.explanation: The lecture uses an over-spread dimension as an example of why data needs exploration before clustering.

questions.question: Why might clustering be inappropriate even if a clustering algorithm runs successfully?
choices: The data may not contain natural clusters
Any dataset with missing values must be clustered
An algorithm always discovers meaningful groups
questions.explanation: An algorithm can always produce labels, but exploration may show there is no meaningful cluster structure.

questions.question: Which pair of data issues does Lecture 1 explicitly suggest checking before modelling?
questions.explanation: The slides explicitly ask whether there are outliers or missing values and how they affect an algorithm.

questions.question: Why is visualisation useful when a dataset becomes large?
choices: It can reveal patterns that are hard to grasp from raw rows
It can show every high-dimensional relationship perfectly
questions.explanation: The slide says large data is difficult to comprehend and visualisation helps us see patterns.

questions.question: What is a reasonable goal of plotting high-dimensional data in fewer dimensions?
choices: To retain every detail with no loss
To prove that every variable predicts the target
To turn all variables into categories
To make some structure easier to inspect
questions.explanation: Lower-dimensional plots help us inspect structure, but they do not preserve all information.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the lecturer's message 'Know it before you machine learn it'?
choices: Understand the dataset and its limitations before choosing a model
Choose the most advanced model first, then inspect the data
Skip cleaning if the dataset has many rows
A model can always compensate for incorrect input data
questions.explanation: The lecturer stresses data cleaning and exploration before modelling.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT something a visualisation alone can establish?
questions.explanation: Plots can suggest patterns and unusual values, but an observed association alone does not establish causation.

questions.question: A random forest gives a record ID a high feature-importance score. What should you conclude?
choices: The ID must cause the target outcome
The model cannot use numerical IDs
Investigate whether the ID reflects a real pattern or a recording artefact
All other features should be deleted
questions.explanation: Feature importance shows the model used the column; it does not prove the column carries meaningful or causal information.

questions.question: In the displayed table, impact_num increases 0, 1, 2, and so on. What is the sensible first check before treating it as a predictive feature?
choices: Whether it is only a row number or ordering artefact
Whether it has the same name as the target
Whether it can be plotted as a pie chart
questions.explanation: Sequential values may encode row order rather than a property of the event. Investigate what the column means before using it.

questions.question: What does the complex database diagram illustrate about real-world data?
choices: Every dataset is already one clean modelling table
Only one table can be explored at a time
Useful information may be spread across many related tables
questions.explanation: Real data may need careful understanding and joins before it becomes a usable analysis table.

questions.question: The decision trees split on a column. Does that alone prove the column is a trustworthy real-world predictor?
choices: Yes, because trees cannot split on irrelevant data
No, the split may exploit an accidental pattern in the sample
Yes, if the column contains integers
No, because decision trees never use numerical columns
questions.explanation: A tree can fit patterns in the sample, including identifiers or artefacts. The feature's meaning and generalisation still need checking.

questions.question: Why does the lecturer contrast familiar example datasets with real-life datasets?
choices: To show that real datasets often need more understanding and cleaning
To show that example datasets have no value
To prove every real dataset has missing values
To say models cannot be used outside competitions
questions.explanation: The contrast motivates exploration: real data is often less tidy and more complex than a teaching or competition example.

questions.question: Which column in the displayed table is clearly categorical rather than a numeric measurement or timestamp?
questions.explanation: The cause column contains labels such as Potholes, Speedbump and Car Wash.

questions.question: In the curse of dimensionality, what does a dimension usually mean?
questions.explanation: A dimension is an attribute or feature used to represent an observation.

questions.question: Which problem does Lecture 1 explicitly associate with thousands of dimensions?
questions.explanation: The slide says high-dimensional data is difficult to visualise.

questions.question: What modelling risk does the Lecture 1 slide connect to many dimensions?
questions.explanation: With many features, a model can more easily fit peculiarities of the training data rather than a pattern that generalises.

questions.question: Why does the lecturer mention dimensionality reduction?
choices: To convert all numbers into text
To make high-dimensional data easier to visualise
questions.explanation: The slide introduces dimensionality reduction as a way to make visualisation easier; its methods come later.

questions.question: Which claim about adding features is safest?
choices: More features always improve a model
More features can make overfitting easier
A model cannot use more than three features
questions.explanation: Lecture 1 warns that many dimensions can make overfitting easier, so more features are not automatically better.

questions.question: Does a lower-dimensional visualisation necessarily preserve every detail of the original high-dimensional data?
choices: Only if the data has no outliers
No, reducing dimensions can leave information out
Only if the data has labels
questions.explanation: The purpose is to make inspection easier, but reducing dimensions can discard or hide some information.

questions.question: For the sorted values 2, 2, 3, 5, 18, what are the mean, median and mode?
questions.explanation: The sum is 30, so the mean is 30/5 = 6. The middle value is 3, and 2 occurs most often.

questions.question: If 18 in the values 2, 2, 3, 5, 18 becomes 100, which centre measure changes more?
questions.explanation: The large value pulls the mean upward, while the middle sorted value remains 3.

questions.question: Which measure is the most frequent value?
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that appears most often.

questions.question: What is the relationship between variance and standard deviation?
choices: Variance is the maximum minus minimum
questions.explanation: Variance is the square of standard deviation; standard deviation is the square root of variance.

questions.question: Which denominator appears in the slide's sample standard-deviation formula?
questions.explanation: The slide divides by N - 1 for a sample and by N for a population.

questions.question: Which percentile corresponds to the median?
questions.explanation: The median divides the sorted data in two and corresponds to the 50th percentile.

questions.question: Why should descriptive statistics often be followed by a plot?
choices: A plot proves the data is normal
A summary can hide the distribution's shape and outliers
questions.explanation: The lecturer warns that quick summaries may hide skewness, outliers and other features of the distribution.

questions.question: What does a category count tell you?
questions.explanation: Count is the number of observations in each category.

questions.question: A distribution has a long tail extending to the right. What is its skew?
questions.explanation: Skew is named for the direction of the longer tail: right-tail means positive skew.

questions.question: A distribution is negatively skewed. Where is its longer tail?
questions.explanation: Negative skew means the left tail is longer. Do not name skew by where most observations are.

questions.question: In the slide's left-skewed illustration, which direction is the mean pulled?
questions.explanation: Extreme values in the left tail pull the mean leftward. The diagram places the mean left of the median and mode.

questions.question: Which description best matches a symmetric distribution in the slide's diagram?
questions.explanation: The slide's symmetric example has matching left and right sides, with mean, median and mode aligned.

questions.question: Which measure describes asymmetry rather than tail heaviness?
questions.explanation: Skewness describes left-right asymmetry; kurtosis describes tail heaviness relative to normal.

questions.question: Which kurtosis type has heavier tails than a normal-like distribution?
questions.explanation: Leptokurtic is positive on the slide's excess-kurtosis scale and has heavier tails.

questions.question: Which kurtosis type has lighter tails than normal?
questions.explanation: Platykurtic has negative excess kurtosis and thinner tails than the normal-like curve.

questions.question: On the excess-kurtosis scale used in the slides, what is the normal-like reference called?
questions.explanation: Mesokurtic is the normal-like reference, labelled zero in the slide's diagram.

questions.question: A dataset has many unusually extreme observations relative to a normal-like curve. Which property is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Kurtosis concerns tail heaviness, which relates to extreme observations.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes skewness from kurtosis?
choices: Skewness concerns asymmetry; kurtosis concerns tail heaviness
Skewness counts rows; kurtosis counts columns
Skewness and kurtosis both prove causation
Kurtosis is another name for the median
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts left-right symmetry with the extent of heavy or light tails.

questions.question: Which correlation is stronger in magnitude: -0.9 or +0.4?
choices: -0.9 because its absolute value is larger
questions.explanation: Strength follows absolute value; the negative sign gives direction, not weakness.

questions.question: What does a negative correlation indicate?
choices: As one variable tends to rise, the other tends to fall
Both variables must be negative numbers
One variable definitely causes the other
questions.explanation: The negative sign indicates an inverse association, not negative values or causation.

questions.question: Which coefficient is most directly designed for a linear relationship?
questions.explanation: Pearson correlation describes linear association.

questions.question: A relationship curves upward but never turns downward. Which coefficient is useful for this monotonic pattern?
questions.explanation: Spearman uses ranks and can capture a monotonic relationship even when it is not straight.

questions.question: Why might Spearman correlation be weak for a clear U-shaped relationship?
choices: The relationship changes direction and is not monotonic
questions.explanation: A U-shape falls and then rises, so one consistent rank direction does not describe it well.

questions.question: Pearson correlation is near zero. Which conclusion is safest?
choices: There is no strong linear association detected, but another pattern may exist
The variables cannot be related in any way
One variable has no effect on anything
The data must be normally distributed
questions.explanation: A near-zero Pearson coefficient does not rule out curved or other non-linear relationships.

questions.question: Which other rank-based dependence measure does the slide name alongside Spearman?
questions.explanation: Kendall's tau is similar in purpose to Spearman as a rank-based dependence measure.

questions.question: A coefficient is +0.8. What does the positive sign tell you?
choices: The variables tend to move in the same direction
The first variable causes the second
Each value rises by exactly 0.8 units
questions.explanation: Positive sign indicates same-direction association; 0.8 is not a slope or causal claim.

questions.question: Can a strong correlation alone prove that one variable causes another?
choices: Yes, if both variables are numeric
No, another factor may explain the association
No, because all correlations are weak
questions.explanation: Association does not by itself identify the cause; confounding factors may be present.

questions.question: What is the possible range of a standard correlation coefficient?
questions.explanation: The lecture gives the range as -1 through +1.

questions.question: What does the height of a histogram bar usually show?
questions.explanation: The variable is divided into bins; each bar shows how many observations fall in a bin.

questions.question: What might happen if histogram bins are much too wide?
choices: Small features of the distribution may be hidden
The histogram becomes a scatter plot
questions.explanation: Broad bins merge values together and may conceal structure; bin width is an important choice.

questions.question: What might happen if histogram bins are much too narrow?
choices: The chart may look noisy or fragmented
Every bar must have the same count
questions.explanation: Many very narrow bins can emphasise small fluctuations rather than the broader distribution shape.

questions.question: How does the lecture describe constructing a KDE?
choices: Connect histogram bar tops with straight lines
Replace each value with a box
Place a smooth curve at each data point and combine the curves
questions.explanation: The slide shows a continuous kernel centred on each observation; together they form a smooth density estimate.

questions.question: What does the lecture say is on the KDE y-axis?
questions.explanation: The slide explicitly says probability density, not the probability of one exact value.

questions.question: Which pairing is correct?
choices: Histogram: binned counts; KDE: smoothed density
Histogram: spatial distance; KDE: category count
questions.explanation: A histogram counts observations in intervals, whereas KDE produces a smooth density estimate.

questions.question: A histogram is mainly suited to viewing the distribution of which type of variable?
questions.explanation: The slide presents histograms as an approximate view of the distribution of one continuous variable.

questions.question: Why can overlapping KDE curves be useful?
choices: They prove two groups are identical
They convert all values to counts
They help compare distribution shapes on the same axes
questions.explanation: The slide notes KDE is useful when comparing distributions together on shared axes.

questions.question: What does the line inside a standard box plot usually mark?
questions.explanation: The line inside the box marks the median, the middle sorted value.

questions.question: Which values form the lower and upper edges of the box?
questions.explanation: The box runs from Q1 to Q3, containing the middle half of the observations.

questions.question: Do box-plot whiskers always end at the exact observed minimum and maximum?
choices: No, their meaning depends on the plotting rule
Only when the data is categorical
questions.explanation: The slide notes alternative whisker conventions, including standard-deviation or percentile limits.

questions.question: What do separate dots beyond the box-plot whiskers commonly indicate?
questions.explanation: Points beyond the whiskers are commonly drawn separately as potential outliers; they need investigation, not automatic deletion.

questions.question: What does the width of a violin at a particular value suggest?
choices: Relative density or concentration of observations
The exact number of missing rows
questions.explanation: The violin adds a KDE-like shape; wider regions indicate more concentrated values.

questions.question: Which plot is especially useful for seeing multiple peaks in a distribution?
questions.explanation: The violin's density shape can show multimodality that a compact box summary may hide.

questions.question: Which statement best compares box and violin plots?
choices: Box plots emphasise quartiles and outliers; violins also show density shape
Box plots always reveal every peak
questions.explanation: A box plot is a compact five-number-style summary; a violin adds a density view.

questions.question: Which section of a box plot contains the middle 50% of values?
choices: The box between Q1 and Q3
questions.explanation: Q1 to Q3 spans the central half of the ordered data.

questions.question: What does colour represent in a heatmap?
choices: The order in which rows were recorded
The name of the plotting library
questions.explanation: The lecture defines heatmaps as using colour to display the magnitude of values.

questions.question: You want to compare correlations across many pairs of numerical variables. Which plot is most suitable?
questions.explanation: A matrix heatmap uses rows and columns for variable pairs and colour for the corresponding correlation values.

questions.question: In a spatial heatmap, what is colour tied to?
choices: The magnitude of a value at a location
The alphabetical order of place names
The number of variables in the entire dataset
The age of the map file
questions.explanation: A spatial heatmap displays values over locations, with colour encoding magnitude at each place.

questions.question: Why should you read a heatmap's colour scale before interpreting it?
choices: Because every heatmap uses the same colours
Because a colour has no universal value meaning
questions.explanation: Colour represents magnitude, but the legend defines which colours correspond to larger or smaller values in that plot.

questions.question: Which is a difference between a matrix and a spatial heatmap?
choices: Only the spatial heatmap uses colour
A matrix arranges values by rows and columns; a spatial heatmap arranges them by location
A spatial heatmap can only show correlations
A matrix heatmap cannot show missing values
questions.explanation: The lecture shows matrix heatmaps for tables such as correlations or missingness, and spatial heatmaps for values at locations.

questions.question: Which plot best shows the relationship between two numerical variables for individual observations?
questions.explanation: A scatter plot positions each observation using two numerical axes, making their relationship visible.

questions.question: How can a scatter plot include a third categorical variable, such as penguin species?
choices: By changing every point to a bar
By colouring points according to category
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that a categorical third variable can be added; distinct point colours can show its classes.

questions.question: A scatter plot shows two variables increasing together. What is the safest conclusion?
choices: The first variable definitely causes the second
The second variable definitely causes the first
They appear associated, but causation is not established
A third variable cannot affect them
questions.explanation: The plotted association could reflect another variable or coincidence; the scatter plot alone cannot establish causation.

questions.question: What can a scatter plot help reveal beyond an overall upward or downward pattern?
choices: The exact cause of each observation
The correct unit for every variable
questions.explanation: Individual plotted points can reveal separated groups or unusual observations as well as an overall relationship.

questions.question: Which plot choice best fits each aim: many pairwise correlations, then two numeric variables as individual points?
questions.explanation: A matrix heatmap summarises many variable pairs, while a scatter plot shows the two-variable observations directly.

questions.question: What does a dendrogram primarily show?
choices: The exact probability of each observation
questions.explanation: A dendrogram represents how objects or groups connect in a hierarchy.

questions.question: In the lecture's dendrogram, two objects join at a low height. What does this suggest?
choices: They are relatively similar under the chosen distance metric
They are the most different objects
questions.explanation: The slide says lower joining height corresponds to greater similarity under the distance metric.

questions.question: What determines the grouping shown by a dendrogram?
choices: A chosen distance or similarity measure
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that a distance metric is used to group the data.

questions.question: What does the lecture's cluster map add to a heatmap-style view?
choices: A pie chart for every cell
A time axis instead of rows
questions.explanation: The cluster-map slide shows a heatmap together with dendrograms to display similarities among entries.

questions.question: Which chart type does the lecture suggest for comparing counts across categories?
questions.explanation: Bar charts compare the quantities or counts of different categories.

questions.question: A value is measured repeatedly over a long period. Which chart best shows how it changes over time?
questions.explanation: The slide recommends line charts for continuously changing data such as a time series.

questions.question: What are bar and pie charts used for on the lecture's chart-choice slide?
choices: Showing the exact coordinates of observations
questions.explanation: The slide groups bar and pie charts as ways to compare quantities or counts of categories.

questions.question: What does univariate analysis explore?
choices: Only a relationship between two variables
questions.explanation: Univariate means examining a single variable; it may be numerical or categorical.

questions.question: You want to examine the relationship between bill length and flipper length. Is this univariate or bivariate analysis?
choices: Univariate, because one species is plotted
Bivariate, because two variables are involved
Neither, because it needs a map
questions.explanation: Bivariate analysis explores a relationship between two variables, regardless of whether both are numerical.

questions.question: Which combination best explores two numerical variables and a third categorical grouping?
choices: A histogram of one numeric variable only
A pie chart of one category only
A single line chart with no labels
A scatter plot with points coloured by category
questions.explanation: Two numerical axes show the relationship; colour can identify a third categorical variable.

questions.question: A record lists a person's age as -4 years. What is the best first response?
choices: Treat it as an obvious inconsistency and investigate it
Assume every negative value is a useful outlier
Convert the whole age column to text
Keep it because calculations can still run
questions.explanation: A negative age is not plausible; the lecture recommends identifying inconsistencies and deciding how to handle them.

questions.question: Which operation can accidentally multiply rows and produce duplicate observations?
questions.explanation: The slides identify joins and combining sources as common ways duplicate observations arise.

questions.question: How can you find candidate duplicate observations?
choices: Group by relevant identifying columns and count rows
Keep only the first alphabetical category
Plot a single KDE and delete every peak
questions.explanation: Grouping on relevant columns and checking counts can reveal candidates for duplicate review.

questions.question: Two rows look similar but may represent two separate fuel purchases. What should you do before removing either row?
choices: Assume similar rows are always errors
Keep only the row with a higher value
Check whether they are true duplicate records or legitimate repeated events
questions.explanation: Repeated real-world events can be valid; confirm record identity before dropping a suspected duplicate.

questions.question: A category appears as 'Pothole', 'pothole', and 'potholes' with the same intended meaning. What is the sensible cleaning step?
choices: Treat all three as unrelated classes
Delete every row with those labels
Convert them to three numerical features without checking
questions.explanation: The slide uses these labels as an example of classes that should be grouped after checking their meaning.

questions.question: Which chart can help reveal inconsistent labels when there are a manageable number of categories?
questions.explanation: The lecture suggests bar charts for spotting category names that do not make sense or may be duplicates.

questions.question: You are modelling single-family homes only. How should apartment records be treated?
choices: As essential examples for the target population
As irrelevant observations for this specific problem
As evidence that every class label is a typo
As automatic outliers within the home prices
questions.explanation: Whether a record is relevant depends on the problem; the slide gives apartments in a single-family-home task as an exclusion example.

questions.question: What is high bias most associated with on the lecture slide?
choices: A model memorising every training example
A dataset with no missing values
An overly simple model that underfits
questions.explanation: High bias means the model is too simple or misses information, leading to underfitting.

questions.question: A model follows quirks of its training set but performs poorly on new data. Which problem does that illustrate?
questions.explanation: The slide says high variance means paying too much attention to training data and failing to generalise.

questions.question: Why might a value such as 100,000 km driven in one month need a domain check?
choices: It is unusual and may be inconsistent, but its meaning depends on context
Every large number is automatically invalid
It proves the vehicle was driven exactly that far
Only string values can be inconsistent
questions.explanation: The lecture uses implausible monthly mileage as an example of a potential inconsistency that should be investigated with domain knowledge.

questions.question: What does MCAR mean?
choices: Missingness depends on the unseen value
Missingness is explained by a recorded feature
Missingness is unrelated to the values or other variables
questions.explanation: Missing Completely At Random means the chance of being missing is not related to observed or unobserved values.

questions.question: A recorder fails unpredictably, regardless of the vehicle or reading. Which missingness mechanism best fits?
questions.explanation: An unrelated random equipment failure is an example of missing completely at random.

questions.question: Which description best captures MAR in the usual statistical distinction?
choices: Missingness depends only on the missing value itself
Missingness cannot be explained by any variable
Missingness can be explained by observed variables
questions.explanation: Missing At Random does not mean causeless. After accounting for recorded variables, missingness need not depend on the unseen value itself.

questions.question: Fuel-cost values are more often missing for older cars, and car age is recorded. Which mechanism could fit if age explains the missingness?
choices: MNAR because the costs must be high
questions.explanation: Recorded car age can explain the chance that cost is missing, which is the usual MAR situation.

questions.question: People omit a fuel cost specifically because that cost was unusually high, even after considering recorded features. Which mechanism best fits?
questions.explanation: The missingness depends on the cost value that is itself missing, the hallmark of Missing Not At Random.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between MAR and MNAR?
choices: MAR can be accounted for using observed variables; MNAR still depends on the unseen value
MAR means values are never missing; MNAR means all values are missing
MAR applies only to text; MNAR only to numbers
MAR is always harmless; MNAR always makes analysis impossible
questions.explanation: For MAR, observed data can explain the missingness; for MNAR, missingness depends on the missing value even after accounting for observed data.

questions.question: Why should you investigate which rows are missing a value before choosing a treatment?
choices: Because every blank cell has the same cause
Because missingness patterns can carry information or bias the analysis
Because plots are impossible with any missing value
Because all missing rows must be deleted
questions.explanation: The lecture asks us to look for a sensible root cause; the pattern affects how we interpret and handle missing data.

questions.question: Does 'Missing At Random' mean that missing values have no identifiable pattern at all?
choices: Yes; MAR is another name for MCAR
Yes; MAR means nothing is missing
No; the pattern may be explained by recorded variables
questions.explanation: The name is deceptive: MAR missingness may depend on observed information, unlike MCAR.

questions.question: If some values are missing, what conclusion does the lecture support?
choices: The impact can be serious, but investigate the cause before deciding what to do
Delete the entire variable without inspection
questions.explanation: Missing values can affect analysis, but the slide explicitly says they do not automatically make it impossible.

questions.question: When might deleting rows with missing values be more defensible according to the lecture?
choices: When the missingness is MCAR and the remaining sample is still adequate
Whenever any column has a blank
Only when the dataset has one category
questions.explanation: Deletion can be considered under MCAR, but it still loses observations and needs a sample-size check.

questions.question: What is a direct cost of deleting rows with missing values?
choices: Sample size and statistical power can decrease
questions.explanation: Fewer observations can mean less power even when deletion is otherwise acceptable.

questions.question: Why is median imputation often preferable to mean imputation when observed values have extreme outliers?
choices: The median is less pulled by extreme values
The median preserves every correlation exactly
The median removes all missingness mechanisms
questions.explanation: Extreme observations can pull the mean much more than the median, so the median may be a more representative fill value.

questions.question: A dataset contains two groups with very different typical fuel costs. Why might one global mean be a poor fill value?
choices: It makes every missing value MCAR
It may represent neither group's typical value well
questions.explanation: The slide notes that sub-populations can have different means; a single overall value can hide that structure.

questions.question: What can filling all gaps with one constant do to a variable's distribution?
choices: Create a pile-up at the fill value and distort spread
questions.explanation: Repeatedly inserting the same value changes the observed distribution and can reduce or distort variation.

questions.question: Which statement about constant-value imputation and relationships is most accurate?
choices: It can distort relationships with other variables
It always makes every correlation exactly zero
It proves the missingness is random
questions.explanation: Filling with a constant can alter correlations and modelling outcomes; it does not literally force every correlation to zero.

questions.question: How does regression imputation obtain a missing value?
choices: It selects the global median without using other features
It copies a value from a separate dataset
It predicts from other observed variables
questions.explanation: A regression model uses the remaining observed variables to predict a missing entry.

questions.question: What limitation does the lecture note for plain regression imputation?
choices: It can only fill text labels
A fixed prediction does not include the value's natural residual variation
It always requires a separate dataset
questions.explanation: A deterministic prediction omits the natural variability around the regression estimate.

questions.question: Hot-deck imputation chooses a value from where?
choices: A similar record in the same dataset
questions.explanation: Hot-deck finds records with similar other variables in the current dataset and draws a donor value.

questions.question: What distinguishes cold-deck from hot-deck imputation in these slides?
choices: Cold-deck draws from a separate dataset
questions.explanation: Cold-deck uses an external dataset as the source of donor values; hot-deck uses the current dataset.

questions.question: What does NaN often indicate in a numerical column?
questions.explanation: NaN means Not a Number and often appears where a numeric value is missing or undefined.

questions.question: Why check how an aggregation function treats NaN?
choices: It always converts NaN to infinity
It may silently omit NaN values, changing the count used
It proves the column is categorical
questions.explanation: The slide warns that counts, sums, and other aggregations may skip NaNs, so you should verify the effective sample.

questions.question: An age column contains -1. What should you check before treating it as a real age?
choices: Whether -1 is a sentinel for unknown or erroneous age
Whether the row is first in the file
Whether every age should be scaled to -1
Whether the chart colour is red
questions.explanation: Negative age is not physically valid; the slide uses it as a possible marker for unknown age.

questions.question: What is a sentinel value such as 999 sometimes used for?
choices: Proving a value is an outlier
Showing that all records have the same value
Marking an error or missing value when 999 is not plausible
questions.explanation: Values such as -1 or ±999 may be placeholders when that number cannot reasonably occur in the field.

questions.question: Should every occurrence of -1 or 999 automatically be converted to missing?
choices: Yes, those numbers are never valid
Only if the dataset has a time column
No; first check the column's meaning and documentation
Yes, but only for categorical variables
questions.explanation: A sentinel interpretation depends on context; a number can be a valid measurement in another column.

questions.question: Which calculation can produce positive or negative infinity in numerical data?
choices: Finding a median of five finite numbers
questions.explanation: The lecture specifically warns that ±infinity can arise from divide-by-zero errors and needs investigation.

questions.question: Why might placeholder values like -999 distort an outlier check?
choices: They are always close to the mean
They can look extremely far from genuine values despite representing missingness
They prevent all plots from rendering
They prove the sample has high bias
questions.explanation: A sentinel can appear as an extreme observation unless it is recognised and handled as a placeholder.

questions.question: You find +infinity in a derived rate column. What is the sound first step?
choices: Assume it is an ordinary finite observation
Replace all rates with the mean immediately
Check the calculation and whether its denominator was zero
questions.explanation: The slide recommends investigating whether divide by zero produced the infinite value before choosing a treatment.

questions.question: A value lies far from the rest of the distribution. What should you conclude first?
choices: It is definitely a recording error
It has no effect on visualisations
It is a potential outlier whose meaning needs investigation
questions.explanation: The lecture says outliers can affect plots and models but should not automatically be discarded.

questions.question: Why might deleting an unusual observation be especially harmful in rare-event analysis?
choices: It may be the very event the analysis aims to find
It would always increase sample size
It would guarantee a normal distribution
It would make all other values identical
questions.explanation: A genuine rare event can be the signal of interest, so its context matters before removal.

questions.question: How can an extreme observation affect a visualisation?
choices: It can stretch the axis and hide detail among typical values
It changes every value into a category
questions.explanation: An extreme value can influence the plot scale and make most observations difficult to distinguish.

questions.question: What is 'masking' in the outlier discussion?
choices: Replacing all values with the mean
Hiding category names on a graph
An extreme value affecting the reference scale so other unusual values are harder to notice
questions.explanation: An extreme observation can influence spread or thresholds and conceal other unusual points; reassessment may reveal them.

questions.question: Which outlier rule examines values in the top and bottom chosen portions of a distribution?
questions.explanation: Percentile-based screening uses chosen upper and lower cutoffs in the ordered values.

questions.question: When is a simple Z-score rule most naturally justified by the slide?
choices: When no observations have a mean
When the sample contains only one row
When the numerical distribution is roughly Gaussian
questions.explanation: The slide discusses standard-deviation distance from the mean in the context of a Normal or Gaussian distribution.

questions.question: Which plot can quickly reveal an unusual point in a two-numerical-variable view?
questions.explanation: The lecture notes scatter plots as a quick visual outlier check in two dimensions.

questions.question: What assumption about outliers underlies isolation forest on the lecture slide?
choices: They must form the largest cluster
They are relatively rare and far from other points
They always occur in time series
questions.explanation: Isolation forest uses trees and works from the idea that anomalous points are rare and easier to isolate.

questions.question: Which outlier methods on the slide use distance or neighbourhood structure?
choices: A pie chart and a line chart
questions.explanation: The slide lists KNN and DBSCAN as distance-metric-based approaches.

questions.question: After investigating a genuine extreme value, which choices does the lecture allow?
choices: Remove it, keep it, or cap it depending on the problem
questions.explanation: The decision depends on whether the value is error, meaningful rare event, or a value needing a justified limit.

questions.question: What is the main idea behind 'better data beats fancier algorithms' on the lecture slide?
choices: The quality and representation of features can matter more than a complex model
Every simple model is always more accurate
Adding more columns always improves accuracy
questions.explanation: A useful representation can expose patterns a model might not discover easily from the raw columns.

questions.question: Which action is feature engineering?
choices: Keeping only the best three existing columns
Deleting every row with a blank
Computing capture delay from captured and fuelled dates
questions.explanation: Feature engineering creates a useful new feature from existing raw information.

questions.question: What does feature selection do after candidate features have been created?
choices: Guarantees every feature is normally distributed
Chooses an informative subset and reduces unnecessary dimensions
Replaces every feature with its mean
questions.explanation: Selection aims to retain informative features and discard irrelevant or redundant ones.

questions.question: Why can adding all available features make a model worse?
choices: More features always reduce training time
Every added column is a duplicate
Some features add noise, redundancy, or unnecessary complexity
questions.explanation: The slide warns that extra columns may be pure noise or repeat existing information.

questions.question: Which feature is redundant rather than simply irrelevant?
choices: A second column containing nearly the same information as another useful feature
A random ID unrelated to the task
A column of pure measurement noise
A feature with no relation to any useful pattern
questions.explanation: A redundant feature repeats information already supplied by another feature.

questions.question: What is a transformation of a feature?
choices: A guarantee that the target is correct
A new representation, shape, or scale of the feature
A new observation copied from another dataset
A proof that the feature is causal
questions.explanation: The lecture describes preprocessing transformations as putting existing data into a new representation.

questions.question: Why does the slide prefer transformations that are invertible?
choices: They always make the data normal
They can be reversed to recover original units or values
questions.explanation: Invertibility lets you relate transformed results back to the original representation.

questions.question: Which method is generally most sensitive to differences in feature scale?
questions.explanation: Distance-based methods can let a large-scale feature dominate the distance calculation.

questions.question: Which model family does the slide describe as relatively insensitive to feature scaling?
questions.explanation: Tree-based models split on feature values and are usually much less affected by scaling than distance-based methods.

questions.question: When does the lecture suggest considering a log transformation?
choices: When positive data spans several orders of magnitude
Only when the feature is categorical
Only when a plot is already symmetric
questions.explanation: Logging can compress a wide range of positive magnitudes, especially when values span orders of magnitude.

questions.question: What input restriction does the slide state for Box-Cox?
choices: Values must have a mean of zero
questions.explanation: The slide says Box-Cox is only used with positive values; zero and negative values do not meet that requirement.

questions.question: Does applying a log or Box-Cox transformation guarantee a normal distribution?
choices: Yes, if there are any outliers
Only when the dataset has categories
questions.explanation: Transformations can improve shape or scale but do not guarantee that the result is normal.

questions.question: Which formula standardises an observed value x using its feature's mean and standard deviation?
questions.explanation: A z-score subtracts the feature mean and divides by its standard deviation.

questions.question: After standardising a nonconstant feature using its own mean and standard deviation, what are its resulting mean and standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Subtracting the mean centres the feature at zero; dividing by standard deviation makes its spread one.

questions.question: Does z-score standardisation automatically make a strongly skewed feature Gaussian?
choices: No; it changes centre and scale, not the underlying shape
Only if the feature is categorical
questions.explanation: A skewed distribution remains skewed after a linear shift and rescale.

questions.question: Under min-max scaling to [0, 1], what happens to the smallest and largest observed values used to fit the scale?
questions.explanation: The fitted minimum maps to zero and the fitted maximum maps to one.

questions.question: What does 'unit-norm normalisation' specifically target?
choices: A mean of zero for every feature
questions.explanation: Unit-norm scaling divides a vector by its norm; it is not the same operation as min-max scaling.

questions.question: Which statement keeps the slide's two uses of 'normalisation' clear?
choices: Min-max and unit-norm scaling are identical
Min-max targets a range; unit-norm targets vector length
questions.explanation: The slide mentions a 0-to-1 range and unit norm, but these are distinct scaling methods.

questions.question: Why is scaling especially relevant before nearest-neighbour analysis?
choices: Distance can be dominated by a feature with much larger units
Nearest neighbours ignores all numerical features
Trees require every feature to have unit norm
questions.explanation: Nearest-neighbour methods compare distances, so unbalanced feature scales can skew the comparison.

questions.question: Which model family on the slides is usually less sensitive to feature scaling than nearest neighbours?
questions.explanation: Trees use threshold splits rather than a cross-feature distance, making ordinary rescaling less important.

questions.question: What is an indicator feature?
choices: A guarantee that a model is accurate
A replacement for every original column
A yes/no flag marking whether a condition holds
A plot showing only missing values
questions.explanation: An indicator marks a meaningful condition or group, often using binary values such as 0 and 1.

questions.question: An age threshold flags whether a person met a vaccination eligibility rule at that time. What kind of feature is this?
questions.explanation: The lecture uses age-based eligibility as an example of creating an indicator from a threshold.

questions.question: A housing dataset flags homes with exactly two bedrooms and one bathroom. What does this illustrate?
choices: Guaranteed high rent for every flagged home
Replacing all numeric features with dates
Combining existing conditions into one indicator
questions.explanation: An engineered flag can express a useful combination of several raw features without claiming a guaranteed outcome.

questions.question: A mall's foot traffic drops during lockdown. What can a lockdown indicator add to the analysis?
choices: Proof that the sensor is broken
A guarantee that no other factors matter
A replacement for the entire time series
questions.explanation: The lecture's mobility example shows how domain knowledge about a special event can explain an unusual pattern.

questions.question: Which event could sensibly be represented by an indicator when modelling daily traffic?
choices: The number of decimal places in an unrelated field
questions.explanation: The slide lists holidays, lockdowns, and riots as special events that can affect traffic.

questions.question: Referral labels include website, app, and phone. Which new indicator matches the lecture's grouping idea?
choices: A separate random number for each customer
A flag that every customer was referred by phone
A flag for online versus telephonic signup
A column containing the current time
questions.explanation: The slide suggests grouping signup sources into an online-versus-telephonic indicator.

questions.question: A bus-arrival timestamp includes microseconds, but arrival patterns vary mainly by hour. What is a useful feature to extract?
choices: The full timestamp as an arbitrary ID
questions.explanation: The lecture suggests decomposing timestamps at the granularity relevant to the problem, such as hour or part of day.

questions.question: Which set contains only possible date/time features extracted from a timestamp?
choices: Day of week, hour, part of day
questions.explanation: A timestamp can be decomposed into useful time components rather than used only as a raw string.

questions.question: Why are an extracted 'hour of day' column and a holiday flag examples of feature engineering?
choices: They are new, potentially useful features created from existing data or domain knowledge
They remove all uncertainty from the target
They are both mandatory for every model
questions.explanation: Both represent existing information in a form that may expose a useful pattern to analysis.

questions.question: What is a sparse class in a categorical feature?
choices: A class with very few observations
A class with the largest numerical value
A class that is always missing
questions.explanation: The slide defines sparse classes as categories represented by very few observations.

questions.question: Why can a category represented by only two training rows cause trouble?
choices: It forces all other rows to be deleted
It cannot be stored in a table
A model may fit those few examples rather than a general pattern
questions.explanation: Very rare classes can encourage overfitting because there is little evidence about their general behaviour.

questions.question: What treatment does the lecture suggest for very sparse classes when appropriate?
choices: Assign each rare row its own new class
Convert every category to the same number without checking
questions.explanation: The slide suggests combining sparse categories, but the grouping should respect their meaning.

questions.question: How does one-hot encoding represent a category such as 'BMW'?
choices: As one ranked number where larger brands are better
With a BMW column marked 1 for BMW rows and 0 otherwise
As the average of all car brands
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding creates a binary column for each category.

questions.question: If a categorical feature has 50 distinct values, what can basic one-hot encoding create?
questions.explanation: Basic one-hot encoding produces one 0/1 indicator per category, so many categories lead to many columns.

questions.question: What is a risk of label-encoding nominal car brands as 0, 1, 2, and so on?
choices: It creates one column per brand
It turns every brand into the same class
A model may incorrectly treat the codes as a meaningful order
questions.explanation: Car brands have no inherent numerical ranking, but integer codes may imply one to some models.

questions.question: Which category set genuinely has an order that a numeric encoding could reflect?
questions.explanation: The slide uses bad/okay/good as an ordinal example, unlike nominal brand names.

questions.question: What is the principal column-count difference between basic one-hot and label encoding?
choices: Both create one column per observation
Label encoding always creates more columns
One-hot creates a column per category; label encoding keeps one coded column
questions.explanation: One-hot expands categories into binary columns; label encoding replaces the original labels with numbers in one column.

questions.question: You group several rare but related publisher names before one-hot encoding. What can this help with?
choices: Guaranteeing every publisher has the same sales
Removing the need to inspect categories
Reducing extremely thin classes and the number of dummy columns
questions.explanation: Sensible grouping can reduce sparse classes and the dimensionality created by one-hot encoding.

questions.question: What makes a categorical feature high-cardinality?
choices: It has a very large number of distinct categories
It contains many rows regardless of category count
It has a high numerical mean
questions.explanation: Cardinality refers to the number of distinct category values, not the total number of records.

questions.question: Which comparison is correct?
choices: Sparse and high-cardinality mean exactly the same thing
A sparse class has many rows; high cardinality means one category
Sparse class means few observations in a class; high cardinality means many classes in a feature
questions.explanation: Sparse describes how little data a particular class has; cardinality describes how many distinct classes the feature has.

questions.question: What problem can one-hot encoding thousands of individual ZIP codes create?
choices: A huge set of mostly-zero columns
It converts all rows to missing
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding creates a separate binary attribute per category, which can become unwieldy for high-cardinality features.

questions.question: Which alternative does the slide suggest for many individual IP-address categories?
choices: Make every IP its own target label
Delete every record with an IP
Treat IP addresses as car brands
questions.explanation: Binning individual addresses into IP ranges can reduce the number of distinct categories.

questions.question: How might ZIP codes be transformed into fewer, meaningful geographic categories?
choices: Replace them all with a random number
Convert each one to a separate date
questions.explanation: The slide suggests geocoding ZIP codes to suburbs rather than representing every code separately.

questions.question: What does a supervised-ratio encoding try to represent for each category?
choices: Its association with a defined positive target class
questions.explanation: The slide describes assigning each category a score related to the probability of the positive class.

questions.question: Before interpreting a weight-of-evidence score, what must be defined?
choices: The event and non-event target classes
questions.explanation: The sign of a WoE score only has meaning relative to the chosen event versus non-event.

questions.question: Under the lecture slide's convention, what does a positive WoE score indicate?
choices: A higher share of the defined event for that category
The category is numerically larger than all others
questions.explanation: The slide states that positive WoE corresponds to a higher percentage of the event, once the event is defined.

questions.question: What do supervised ratio and weight of evidence have in common here?
choices: They always create one dummy column per category
They use the target outcome to score categories
questions.explanation: Both are target-based ways to encode categories as scores instead of expanding them into many one-hot columns.

questions.question: What does discretisation do to a numerical feature?
choices: Splits it into categories or intervals
Changes every value to the mean
questions.explanation: The lecture describes turning numerical values into binary or ordered/nominal groups, such as below versus above a threshold.

questions.question: Which property defines equal-width bins?
choices: Each bin has exactly the same number of rows
Each bin has the same class balance
Each bin has the same numerical interval size
Each bin has the same average target
questions.explanation: Equal-width binning uses equal spans of the feature's numeric range; observation counts can differ.

questions.question: Which property defines equal-frequency bins?
choices: Roughly equal numbers of observations per bin
A fixed target value in every bin
questions.explanation: Equal-frequency binning aims to distribute observations fairly evenly, even if the numeric intervals have different widths.

questions.question: Values are very concentrated at the low end of a range. What can happen with equal-width bins?
choices: All bins are guaranteed equally populated
The method uses the target labels by definition
Some bins may be crowded while others contain few observations
questions.explanation: Equal-width spans do not adapt to where observations actually lie, so counts may be very uneven.

questions.question: What criterion does entropy-based splitting seek at each split on the slide?
questions.explanation: The slide compares entropy-based binning with decision-tree splits chosen for maximum information gain.

questions.question: If only overall vehicle sales matter, how can sales_cars and sales_bakkies be crossed?
choices: Add them to form total sales
Replace both with a random ID
questions.explanation: The lecture's sum example combines car and bakkie sales into an overall vehicle-sales feature.

questions.question: Which operation creates 'time on market' from listing and purchase dates?
choices: Listing date multiplied by purchase date
Counting the number of houses in the suburb
questions.explanation: A date difference measures the elapsed time between listing and purchase.

questions.question: Expected purchases are 200 and expected profit per purchase is R15. Which interaction gives expected earnings?
questions.explanation: The product of expected uptake and profit per sale estimates total earnings.

questions.question: To create spending per client from total spending and client count, which operation is appropriate?
choices: Divide total spending by client count
questions.explanation: A quotient turns a total into a per-client rate, matching the slide's interaction example.

questions.question: Why create crossed features rather than only feeding raw columns to a model?
choices: Every feature must be a product
A meaningful combination can expose an interaction based on domain knowledge
questions.explanation: Feature crossing encodes useful relationships between existing variables that may be less obvious separately.

questions.question: How could a driving-behaviour dataset be augmented using a date column?
choices: Replace every date with the target
Join weather observations for the same dates
Convert each date to an arbitrary user ID
questions.explanation: The slide gives weather on a given day as information that can be layered onto time-indexed driving data.

questions.question: What does geocoding a street address produce in the lecture example?
questions.explanation: Geocoding converts an address or place into geographic coordinates.

questions.question: After obtaining latitude and longitude for two places, what new feature might be calculated?
choices: The exact causal effect of location
The number of missing text fields
questions.explanation: Coordinates can be used to compute a geographic distance, for example with the haversine formula.

questions.question: What can a text-embedding model produce from sentences or transaction descriptions?
questions.explanation: Embeddings encode text into numerical vectors that can be compared or clustered.

questions.question: After clustering text embeddings, which result becomes a categorical feature on the slide?
choices: The cluster assignment for each record
The mere fact that two words look similar
questions.explanation: The slide's pipeline is text to embeddings to clusters; the assigned cluster label is used as a new categorical feature.

questions.question: Why ask whether a new feature can be computed for future observations?
choices: Because past values are always useless
Because future rows must have every possible category
Because model predictions will need that feature at the time they are made
Because the feature must be normally distributed
questions.explanation: A feature that exists only after the outcome is known cannot be supplied for genuine future predictions.

questions.question: Which is a useful question to ask before keeping a newly engineered feature?
choices: Does it make every row unique?
Does it have the longest name?
Does it always use a neural network?
Is it explainable and potentially predictive?
questions.explanation: The checklist asks whether a feature is intuitive, grounded in knowledge or exploration, and predictive.

questions.question: Why is a feature calculated from the target value invalid for genuine prediction?
choices: It always has too few categories
It leaks the answer, which will not be available when predicting new cases
It must have a mean of zero
questions.explanation: The slide explicitly warns not to use the target to build features: it gives the model information unavailable in production.

questions.question: You predict whether a future refuelling will be expensive before it happens, but use the final receipt's total_spent as an input. What is the problem?
choices: Target leakage, because the feature reconstructs the answer
questions.explanation: The final receipt is not available before the refuelling; using it gives away information about the outcome.
